SUPERIOR COURT:
a. Consideration of the appointment of David Widmaier to fill the vacancy for
the remainder of the term as Justice of the Peace, Precinct Six, effective
February 8, 2026, due to the retirement of the Honorable Robert J.
Higgins.
Chairman Seymore invited Judge Higgins to the podium while
congratulating him on his retirement.
Judge Higgins thanked the Board for the opportunity to come before them
and expressed thanks to them for appointing him 5 years ago to be the
Justice of the Peace, after serving in Superior Court for the 9 years prior.
He explained that he has been working in Navajo County for 31 years,
either practicing law or serving as a Judge.  He stated that he has had a
great career and enjoyed working with everyone in Navajo County. Judge
Higgins thanked Judge Little, the Presiding Judge of Justices of the
Peace.  He also thanked Judge Ruechel, stating that he enjoyed working
with her. He went on to thank Joel Ruechel, his first mentor, and called
him a walking encyclopedia of Arizona law.  He acknowledged County
Attorney Brad Carlyon, who was his first partner when he went into private
practice. Judge Higgins then recommended David Widmaier to take his

place for the interim year, stating that he had previously served as the

b. Recognition of the Honorable Robert J. Higgins, Justice of the Peace
Precinct Six, on his retirement.
Judge Michala Ruechel thanked the Board for the opportunity to honor
Judge Higgins.  Judge Ruechel shared a quote from James Keller, “A
candle loses nothing by lighting another candle”, explaining that Judge
Higgins is the embodiment of that saying and that he is a bright candle who
has made a mission of lighting other candles. Judge Ruechel explained
that Judge Higgins started as a teacher in Micronesia and then Phoenix.
After he finished law school, he moved to Navajo County and has worked
in the community for more than 30 years.  She said that he has worked in
private practice, the County Attorney’s Office, he has served as a Superior
Court Judge, and a Justice of the Peace.  She went on to explain that
Judge Higgins and his wife were instrumental in founding St. Anthony’s
School and continue to be a strong presence there. Judge Higgins was
appointed to the Superior Court by Judge Brewer in 2012. He was
instrumental in getting the South County Court Complex up and running,
later agreeing to become the Justice of the Peace when Judge Widmaier
retired.  Judge Ruechel stated that Judge Higgins mission and goal is to
serve others and to make sure everyone gets and knows justice. She went
on to say that he is one of the kindest, most positive people she has met
and that he has worked hard to serve the community, his family, and the
Lord and that he will continue to be a bright and shining candle and always
light the path for others, and that he will be missed.
Judge Higgins thanked Judge Ruechel for her kind words. He said that he
retires with some sadness and that he has loved his job. He plans to
spend time with grandkids and at St. Anthony’s, he stated that he has
enjoyed his 31 years at Navajo County and the last 14 as a Judge and that
he is looking forward to the future.
Vice Chairwoman Whitesinger congratulated Judge Higgins and thanked
him for his years of service. She said that he has touched many lives and
empowered many people to work towards their greatest potential, even her
own children. She stated that her family has known Judge Higgins since
her oldest was in pre-K and he has touched the lives of and mentored her
children, stating those impacts are close to her heart.  She said that many
in Navajo County have similar stories as he took the time to know the ones
he works with and serves the youth.  She said that she is grateful for his
example and wished congratulations and thanks to his wife Laura as well.
Supervisor Whiting recognized that Judge Higgins is respected by his
peers and those that are in his courtroom.  He said that he appreciated his
thoughtful recommendation of a new judge and congratulated him on his
retirement and thanked him for his service.

NAVAJO COUNTY PUBLIC HEALTH SERVICES DISTRICT: Board of Directors

REGULAR AGENDA:
1. Consideration and adoption of a proclamation declaring the week of
January 18th—January 24th, 2025, as National Medicolegal Death
Investigation Professionals week in Navajo County, Arizona.
Rhonda Krouse greeted the Board and explained that the Navajo County
Medical Examiners program operates quietly, often out of the public view,
but that its role is essential to public safety, public health and the justice
system.  She said that in 2025, their office handled 273 cases each
representing a community member and that they work alongside law
enforcement, mortuaries, healthcare providers and families to ensure that
5 of 14 
Draft

<!-- page 11 -->
enforcement, mortuaries, healthcare providers and families to ensure that
deaths are investigated thoroughly and objectively, that evidence is
preserved, that public health data is accurate, and that answers are
provided when possible.  She explained that they speak for those who no
longer speak for themselves.  Ms. Krouse praised her team that shows up
after hours, on weekends and holidays, oftentimes to emotional cases and
that they do it with consistency, humility, and a deep sense of
responsibility. The team accepts the burden with professionalism and
compassion, so that the families do not have to. Ms. Krouse shared a
message that she believes captures the essence of their work that reads:
“Tonight while homes glow with lights, tables are set and families gather,
there are others who continue their watch. Christmas Eve doesn’t pause
for death, it doesn’t pause for grief, and it doesn’t pause for the
responsibility to care for those left behind. To the investigators, medical
examiners, transport teams, dispatchers, and all who stand in the quiet
after the sirens fade, we see you if you’re on call, on scene, or simply
carrying the weight of what you’ve seen this year.  Know that you are not
alone.  Peace to those who serve, comfort to those who grieve, and
strength to those who carry the final responsibility." Ms. Krouse stated that
in 2025 they had a lot of emotionally trying cases, including 9 homicides,
21 suicides, 11overdoses, 5 first responder deaths, and 28 motor vehicle
deaths to name a few. Ms. Krouse read the proclamation and then
introduced her team, Matthew Player, Jennifer Laws, Anthony Lopez, and
Ryanne Hale. She then thanked the Board on behalf of Navajo County
Public Health for recognizing them today and thanked them for supporting
the work they do every day in the community.
Chairman Seymore thanked Rhonda for the presentation and said that he
appreciates what she and her team do because he knows that it is very
challenging.
Supervisor Whiting thanked Rhonda and her team.  He said that it is
surprising to him how many people there are that don’t realize all that the
County does and that these proclamations help highlight the important
services that are being done by people who authentically care and are
dealing with situations that matter. He admires how they strike a balance of
honoring families and doing their job in a meaningful way.
Supervisor Whiting made a motion to approve declaring the week of
January 18th—January 24th, 2025, as National Medicolegal Death
Investigation Professionals week in Navajo County, Arizona., motion
seconded by Vice Chairwoman Whitesinger.  Vote 4-0 approving the
motion with Supervisor Peshlakai not voting.

3. Presentation to introduce the 2026 Navajo County Community Health
Needs Assessment Survey (CHNAS).
Ciera Hensley, Deputy Health Director for Navajo County, greeted the
Board, expressing her excitement to share information about the upcoming
Community Health Needs Assessment Survey (CHNAS) that will be
launching on February 2, 2026. Ciera explained that the survey gives
residents a direct voice in health needs and barriers, and priorities across
the county. The survey ensures that the county’s planning and investments
7 of 14 
Draft

<!-- page 13 -->
are grounded in lived experience and not assumptions. Ciera said that the
survey is a community-wide survey that is done every 3 years and is made
available to Navajo County residents, 18 and older, online or on paper. The
survey will be available from February 2, 2026, through April 30, 2026,
takes 15 minutes to complete, and will cover a variety of health topics
including physical health, social health, mental health, access to
healthcare, cost of healthcare, substance use, and social determinants of
health.  She said that the survey is accessible and designed to provide
meaningful data. The survey follows a framework called the MAPP 2.0
Framework, which stands for Mobilizing for Action through Planning and
Partnerships and includes 3 phases that are important to the process. 
Ciera provided a recap of the last assessment launched in February 2023. 
With the survey data, Navajo County Public Health identified community
health priorities such as STI, social determinant of health, chronic diseases
and mental health, and substance use.  By September 2023, they were
able to publish their community health assessment report to the public and
later release the community health improvement plan. She then stated that
at the beginning of 2024 they were able to launch work groups focused on
the health priorities of the community. She explained that the data from the
survey is important to Navajo County and Public Health because it
strengthens funding and partnerships, strong community input improves
program outcomes, helps in funding applications to align with partners,
and supports our local hospitals.
Next, Ciera focused on how the survey would be advertised, stating that
she and the Health Project Services Manager, Sherry Fish, would be
traveling throughout the county.  She thanked their community partners,
Summit Healthcare, Little Colorado Medical Center, and Changepoint for
their collaboration and Alicia Deets for sharing information on Navajo
County’s social media platforms. Ciera highlighted two competitions, a
photo competition where community members can submit landscape
photos of Navajo County; the winning photos will be added to the final
reports and a competition between the towns and cities of Navajo County
to see which can get the highest number of surveys submitted. Ciera
asked the board to consider sharing information about the survey in their
networks as well.
Supervisor Whiting thanked the Navajo County Public Health team for the
presentation and recognized that the survey is important and takes a lot of
coordination to get the community involved to have a meaningful
assessment.
Chairman Seymore also stated that he appreciated the presentation.
Supervisor Benally made a motion to return to regular session, motion
seconded by Vice Chairwoman Whitesinger.  Vote 4-0 approving the
motion with Supervisor Peshlakai not voting.. 
 
BOARD OF SUPERVISORS:
a. Discussion and possible action regarding a Development Agreement with
SE Cygnus, LLC for the development and operation of an up-to
650-megawatt solar energy facility in Navajo County with.  Pursuant to
A.R.S. §38-431.03(A)(3) the Board may convene in Executive Session to
receive legal advice from its attorney.
Chairman Seymore welcomed County Manager Bryan Layton to the
  
                                                                    8 of 14 
Draft

<!-- page 14 -->
podium, noting that after the presentation, the board may move into
Executive Session to receive legal advice from their attorney.
County Manager Bryan Layton said he would start the presentation with
context and, with the permission of the Board, would invite Planning
Manager Cody Cooper to share some technical details about the project.
Mr. Layton started by answering the question of why renewable energy
products are interested in Navajo County, explaining that Navajo County
does not go out and seek these projects. Mr. Layton said that Navajo
County is a great place with abundant wind and solar resources, existing
infrastructure and transmission lines in place, landowners that are willing to
participate, favorable topography, and the state provides an 80% reduction
in property tax. Mr. Layton shared a graphic illustrating that counties are
required to have a comprehensive plan which is the basis of everything that
is done in planning, zoning, and building; built upon the comprehensive
plan is zoning and corridor plans, site plans, building plans, and then
receiving a certificate of occupancy. Mr. Layton explained that the process
of updating the comprehensive plan was started 2 years ago as required
by state statute. He stated that as they started that process, a review of
ordinances was triggered.  He said that the Board asked staff to start with
the renewable energy ordinance first and that it has now been updated and
completed.  Bryan explained that state statute requires the county to
perform certain types of public outreach when updating the comprehensive
plan.  He shared a slide detailing where, when and how the county
adhered to that and said that beyond what is required by statute, the
county also held community meetings, conducted interviews, and provided
digital tools for residents to provide feedback and their perspective on the
process. He said that the county also held 3 listening sessions in Show
Low, Heber, and Joseph City to hear directly from Navajo County residents.
Mr. Layton stated that from all the input they were able to create a
framework for evaluating renewable projects.  The first step in the review is
to evaluate whether the agreement meets or exceeds all the criterion
standards required by the county ordinance and if so, staff will move on to
looking at the preferred criteria. Mr. Layton explained that the public’s
preferred criteria focused on minimizing visual impact, appropriate location,
use of previously disturbed land with low habitat value or limited
vegetation, and water conservation. He added that the projects should also
provide a community benefit, noting that these criteria formed the
framework used to evaluate the project.  Mr. Layton then invited Cody
Cooper to provide some technical details and an overview of the project
itself.
Cody Cooper greeted the Board and proceeded to go over the staff review
that was completed as part of the submittal for the development agreement
that Planning and Development Services conducted for the components
that had been proposed with the Cygnus Solar Project. Mr. Cooper
highlighted the proposal that includes up to 650 megawatts of photo
photovoltaic solar energy and a 400-megawatt capacity battery energy
storage system with a 200-foot generation tie-in line, located on 3,721
acres located 10 miles north of Snowflake, AZ. Mr. Cooper then went over
the components of the review starting with the design, stating that it met or
exceeded all standards that exist in the Navajo County Zoning Ordinance. 
Next, he went over the signage, stating that the setback standards have
                                                                    9 of 14 
Draft

<!-- page 15 -->
been met or exceeded.  Mr. Cooper stated that the fencing was an
important component to the public, and that perimeter fencing would
incorporate wildlife movement corridors and would include six-to-eight-inch
gaps at the bottom for small wildlife movement as recommended by the
Arizona Game and Fish Department. Mr. Cooper explained that the
developer has agreed to preserve dark sky characteristics using shielded
motion-activated light fixtures and no strobe lighting will be employed
unless specifically required by the FAA. He noted that Navajo County is not
a Dark Sky Community as far as ordinances go, so the lighting exceeds the
ordinance. Mr. Cooper went on to review the road use and setbacks,
stating that they have been reviewed to make sure they will not cause any
major impact on the neighboring properties.  Mr. Copper then explained
that bonds to cover reclamation and restoration will be required prior to
construction and updated every 5 years throughout the duration of the
project if accepted and that the developer has agreed to go to 48 inches
below ground upon decommissioning, which exceeds the industry standard
and the zoning ordinance, which is 3 feet.
Supervisor Whiting asked Mr. Cooper to clarify how the bonding would
work to make sure that if the developer were to become insolvent, the
taxpayers would not have to absorb the cost.
Cody Cooper stated that if the project were to be purchased by another
entity or if it were to be taken over by a financier, the bonding is structured
so that any financial requirements of the original developer will have to be
transferred to the new entity, reiterating that there are contingencies put in
place that will require that bonding to remain throughout the life of the
project, regardless of who is in control of the project or property.
Supervisor Whiting asked Cody to explain in simple terms for the public
why that is an acceptable solution and what bonding entails.
Cody Cooper stated that the bonding will require the amount of money that
has been put together by a professional engineer to decommission the
project and restore it back to the natural state will be held for the duration
of the project.  Mr. Cooper explained that bonding is a way to hold money
for the entirety of the project, regardless of entity, to make sure that there is
not anything left behind with the project and no cost incurred by taxpayers
at a later date.
Mr. Cooper explained that the next step in the review process was to
review the preferred criteria that the Board wanted to employ for the
project. He said that one of the preferred criteria was visual impact and
finding ways to minimize this. Mr. Cooper showed a map and explained
that from the nearest public roadways looking at the project you cannot see
the project because of the topography, that there are hills and other
features that block the view of the project from the public roadways.  Mr.
Cooper went over an additional preferred criterion that the project be cited
near existing substations and transmission lines.  He stated that this
project is right next to the transmission lines and the existing Sugarloaf
Substation.  He then reviewed the preferred water conservation criteria,
stating that the developer has agreed to limit the washing of the panels to
twice a year.
Vice Chairwoman Whitesinger asked about the conservation methods for
water usage and asked if there would be water transported to the site.
Mr. Cooper replied that the applicant can transport water to the site or use
                                                                    10 of 14 
Draft

<!-- page 16 -->
any entitlements on the site that come through the Department of Water
Resources, stating that while in construction it is typical for these projects
to go offsite and fill some water trucks to help with dust control on site.
County Manager Bryan Layton then went over the community benefits of
the project.  He recapped a property tax breakout in Navajo County
showing that 47% of each tax dollar goes to local school districts, 23% to
the fire district, 16% to the Northland Pioneer College District, 8% to the
county, and 6% to secondary districts like flood control, library district, and
public health. Mr. Layton referred to the 80% tax break incentives from the
state for these types of projects.  He then stated that the project would last
for 35 years and that the Assessor has worked with the developer and the
estimated, but subject to change, amount of funding over 35 years would
be, to the Snowflake and Holbrook school districts 20 million dollars,
Northland Pioneer College 5.5 million, the Navajo County general fund 2.2
million, the Flood Control District $783k, the Public Health District $718k,
the Library District $286k, and NAVIT $158k.  He then showed a slide that
explains how, over time, the developer is allowed to depreciate the value of
the assets on the property and the corresponding property tax will go down.
Mr. Layton went over the community impacts, such as the influx of
temporary workers who will provide increased consumerism to support
local business but may place strain on housing code enforcement, public
safety infrastructure, and county finances.  He stated that to combat that
concern, the developer has agreed to provide Navajo County with a
one-time 6-million-dollar contribution, termed a community benefit. Mr.
Layton explained that the first $250,000 would be paid within the first 30
days to the county to start recruiting and developing personnel positions to
mitigate those concerns. The remainder is to be paid within 270 days, and
the Board of Supervisors will review where those funds are sent as part of
the annual budget development process. Mr. Layton then explained that
the project is not located within a fire district, and that the developer is
required by ordinance to create an emergency response plan and a
site-specific safety plan that is reviewed by local entities of state Fire
Marshall and county staff. He said that since the properties are not located
within a fire district, there is no financial contribution from property tax to
the fire districts and, if approved, part of the community benefit contribution
will be provided to Taylor/Snowflake Fire and Medical to support their
operations.  Mr. Layton told the Board that they have been provided with a
copy of the Development Agreement, which is complete with the exception
of appendix E, the decommission plan which the developer needs to
update in order to reconcile with the terms that have been agreed upon by
the developer and planning and development services.
Chairman Seymore shared that this is not a public hearing, but that the
board would allow a few comments for 3 minutes.
Buchannon Davis from Salt River Project (SRP) greeted the Board stating
that his company is a proposed off taker for the project.  Mr. Davis
reminded the Board and the public that SRP is a not-for-profit electric and
water company in Arizona with 2 million customers. He stated that they do
not have a customer base in Navajo County but that they have a significant
amount of workforce at the Cornado plant in St. Johns resides in Navajo
County.  He explained that there is tremendous growth in demand for
utilities across the state, and they are meeting that demand with all kinds of
                                                                    11 of 14 
Draft

<!-- page 17 -->
technologies including natural gas, nuclear, and biomass. Mr. Davis said
that renewable energies have come a long way and are an important tool
in the toolbox, stating that solar and battery storage keeps the lights on
when demand is high and reduces the reliance on costly wholesale
markets. He stated that renewable energies serve as a bridge until we
have future technologies, like nuclear, available.  Mr. Davis said that SRP
appreciates the county’s approach to the agreement that they have a
genuine desire to build a partnership with Navajo County.
Vice Chairwoman Whitesinger asked if the the increased production of
energy over the next 10 years is need-based or is it for storage.
Mr. Davis said that it is need-based due to growth in the population as well
as economic growth.
Vice Chairwoman Whitesinger said that she thinks it is important for the
public to understand that growth is driving the need for more power.
Claire Brophy Bellendir with Aztec Land and Cattle thanked the Board for

AMENDMENT NUMBER 1 TO THE AGREEMENT BETWEEN CLIENT AND KIMLEY -HORN 
AND ASSOCIATES, INC.  
 
 
 This is Amendment number 1 dated ________, 2026 to the agreement between Navajo 
County ("Client") and Kimley -Horn and Associates, Inc. ("Consultant") dated  September 23, 2025  
(“the Agreement") concerning the Navajo County Transportation Master Plan (the "Project"). 
 
The Consultant has entered into the Agreement with Client for the furnishing of professional 
services, and the parties now desire to amend the Agreement.   
 
The Agreement is amended to include services to be performed by Consultant for 
compensation as set forth below in accordance with the terms of the Agreement, whi ch are 
incorporated by reference.  
 
Consultant will perform the following additional services: 
 
Task 1. Project Management 
Task 1.5. Project Closeout Meeting  
Consultant will meet with Client following the adoption/acceptance of the TMP to discuss 
transmitting all electronic files as well as the successes and challenges of the TMP process.  
 
Task 2. Public and Stakeholder Engagement 
 
Task 2.4. Technical Advisory Committee 
Consultant will hold up to three additional virtual TAC meetings at key points in the TMP planning 
process:  
• Review the final project list and input on the project prioritization framework, concurrent 
with Task 4.3 
• Review of draft prioritization results and initial recommendations, concurrent with Task 4.4.  
• Review of the draft final report, concurrent with Task 5.2.  
 
Task 2.5. Board of Supervisors Presentations 
Consultant will provide one additional in -person presentation to the Navajo County Board of 
Supervisors concurrent with Task 5.2 for review and approval of the draft final TMP.  
 
Task 4. Project Prioritization 
Task 4.2. Planning -Level Cost Development  
Consultant will work with Client to develop a list of planning -level unit costs for each improvement 
type. After agreeing to unit costs, Consultant  will develop planning -level cost estimates for each of 
the projects included in the project list in Task 4.1.  
 
Task 4.3. Prioritization Framework 
Using the updated goals and objectives developed in Task 3.1, Consultant will create a measurable 
performance indicator for each objective, which will serve as the basis for project prioritization. 
Consultant will work with Client and the TAC to weigh the TMP goals and emphasize those that 
are most impactful to Navajo County.  
 
Task 4.4. Performance Based Prioritization  
Based on the goals, objectives, and performance indicators, and weighting established in Task 4.3, 
Consultant will develop a spreadsheet -based prioritization tool to objectively rank projects by their 
regional importance and ability to advance the TMP goals. Consultant will work with Client and the 
TAC to review draft results and modify the tool’s inputs as necessary to provide a project list that 
is both technically and politically feasible to implement. This tool will be provided to Client  at the 
conclusi on of the TMP allowing Client to continuously evaluate new projects as they emerge and

<!-- page 26 -->
Rev. 7/18 
priorities evolve after completion of the TMP.  
 
Task 4.6. Policy Recommendations 
Consultant will work with Client to develop applicable policy recommendations to formalize 
recurring issues or requests received by Navajo County Public Works staff.  
 
Task 5. Enhanced Draft and Final Report 
Task 5.1. Draft TMP Development  
Consultant will compile and streamline the contents of Working Papers 1 and 2 into a draft TMP 
document. Consultant will also develop an Executive Summary, which will summarize key 
takeaways from the planning process and recommendations. The draft TMP document will be 
provided to Client  for review.  
 
Task 5.2. Final TMP  
Consultant will address comments provided by Client to create an updated draft TMP document. 
The updated draft will then be circulated to the TAC for review and comment. Consultant will 
document any comments received from the TAC in a comment resolution matrix and work with 
Client to review and approve updates. Another updated draft TMP document will then be produced, 
which will be presented to the Navajo County Board of Supervisors, as described in Task 2.5. If 
any additional comments are received from the Board of Supervisors, Consultant will make 
requested updates to produce a final TMP document and executive summary.  
 
Task 5.3. Project Closeout  
Consultant will provide all final products produced throughout the planning process:  
• Final Working Papers 1 and 2 in both PDF and editable versions  
• Final TMP document and executive summary in both PDF and editable versions  
• Spreadsheet tools developed throughout the planning process  
• GIS data and mapping produced through the planning process  
• Final invoice and progress report

Title: Dark Fiber IRU Agreement
Submitted For: Grant Evans, Director of Facilities and Capital Projects 
Submitted By: Grant Evans, Director of Facilities and Capital Projects
Department: Facilities Mangement
Motion before the Board:
Approval to enter into a Dark Fiber Indefeasible Right of Use (IRU) Agreement with Frontier
Communications of America, Inc.
Background:
On May 13, 2025, the Board of Supervisors (BOS) approved the pricing structure and associated IRU
agreement template for leasing of the Navajo County Middle Mile broadband fiber. Utilizing those
documents, staff and our commercialization partner, eX2 Technology, LLC, have negotiated this Dark
Fiber IRU Agreement with Frontier Communications of America, Inc. This IRU agreement sets forth a
20-year indefeasible right to use four (4) fibers on the county's middle mile network for the entire
106-miles of system routes. The Board previously approved this IRU on December 17, 2025, but the
Grantee later requested a few minor revisions to the agreement.  This agreement supersedes that
agreement from December 17, 2025.  Approval of this IRU is a major step forward in the development
and commercialization of the County's Middle Mile fiber project and will improve and enhance
broadband availability, reliability and capacity throughout our County.
Staff recommends entering into this Dark Fiber IRU Agreement with Frontier Communications of
America, Inc.

Cooperative Agreement
for
Animal Impoundment Services
between
Navajo County and the Town of Snowflake
This Agreement is made as of December 1st, 2025 (the "Effective Date") by and between the
TOWN OF SNOWFLAKE, an Arizona municipal corporation ("TOWN"), and NAVAJO COUNTY
PUBLIC HEALTH, a political subdivision of the State of Arizona ("COUNTY"):
I. RECITALS
1. Both parties are authorized by statute and ordinance to perform animal control activities
within their respective jurisdictions.
2. TOWN owns and operates an Animal Control Center at 600 Snow Blvd. for its own animal
control activities.
3. TOWN is willing to accept seized dogs from COUNTY at its Animal Control Center upon the
terms and conditions set forth herein.
II. AGREEMENT
1. TOWN agrees to give COUNTY access to four of its kennels for impoundment of
animals seized throughout the county. After the 72- hour hold time, the dog becomes
the property of the TOWN to do with as it sees fit.
2. This Agreement shall remain in effect for one year, with the option to renew annually up
to 5 years. See paragraph 7.
3. For each dog accepted for impoundment at TOWN'S Animal Control Center, COUNTY
agrees to pay to TOWN a monthly fee of $1200.00 for animals brought in only by the
COUNTY Animal Care & Control officer. This fee shall be inclusive of all services
typically provided by TOWN in connection with dogs impounded at the Animal Control
Center, including daily care and feeding. This fee may be amended from time to time by
mutual agreement of TOWN and COUNTY, any such amendments shall be in writing
and approved by the COUNTY’s Board of Supervisors and attached hereto.
4. COUNTY understands the $1000.00 fee does not include medical treatment for which
the services of a veterinarian are required.  If such services are required, the COUNTY
will be notified before services and may decide against such services.  If services are
agreed the COUNTY agrees to pay the billed charges.
a. The COUNTY will pay $200 for any dog brought in by a COUNTY Animal Care &
Control officer for rabies observation quarantine unless the dog owner pays all
applicable quarantine fees.
b. The COUNTY agrees to allow the TOWN to keep all impound fees and daily
maintenance fees collected from dog owners on behalf of the COUNTY.

<!-- page 70 -->
5. The TOWN shall bill the COUNTY on a monthly basis. The COUNTY shall make
payment within 15 days after receipt of the TOWN'S invoice unless a charge is
disputed, in which the bill will not be paid until both parties cooperate to promptly
resolve the disputed charge.
                                    Invoices shall be submitted to:
                                                Attn: Navajo County Animal Control
600 N 9th Pl
Show Low, AZ 85901
Payments shall be mailed to:
Attn: Finance Department
81 W 1st South
Snowflake, AZ 85937
6. The TOWN shall exercise the same degree of care with respect to dogs impounded by
COUNTY as it exercises with respect to dogs impounded by its own animal control
officers.
7. This Agreement shall remain in effect for one year, with the option to renew annually up
to 5 years.  Termination of agreement by mutual agreement of the parties or by either
party giving 30 days written notice of termination to the other at the addresses specified
above.  This Agreement is also terminable in accordance with the provisions of A.R.S
38-511, and that statute is hereby incorporated into this Agreement by reference.
8. In the event the TOWN’s Animal Control Center is temporarily unavailable for use due
to maintenance, animal illness/outbreak, or any other condition that renders the facility
unusable for impoundment, the monthly fee charged to the COUNTY shall be pro-rated
for the period during which services are unavailable.
9. In the event that TOWN staff are unavailable to perform essential duties at the Animal
Control Center including but not limited to feeding, watering, cleaning, administering
medications, or conducting euthanasia the COUNTY may, with TOWN's consent, step
in to provide temporary support. Any such assistance provided by COUNTY staff shall
be done without liability to the COUNTY, its employees, or agents.
IN WITNESS WHEREOF, the authorized representatives of the parties have executed this IGA as
of the Effective Date.

Title: Navajo County Continuity of Operations/Continuity of Government Plan 2026-2027
Submitted For: Catrina Jenkins, EMP Director 
Submitted By: Catrina Jenkins, EMP Director
Department: NC Public Health Services District Division: Emergency Management
Motion before the Board:
Navajo County Continuity of Operations and Continuity of Government Plan for 2026-2027
Background:
Navajo County Emergency Management and Preparedness requests approval of the Navajo County
Continuity of Operations (COOP) and Continuity of Government (COG) Plan for the upcoming two
years. The purpose of COOP/COG planning is to minimize the impacts of disasters and emergencies to an
acceptable level and to ensure that Navajo County, Arizona, maintains the capability to continue essential
functions under all conditions.
Each Navajo County department maintains a Continuity of Operations Plan designed to ensure that
critical services and normal business operations can continue during and after an emergency.
Departments have reviewed, updated, and enhanced their individual plans to reflect current operations,
resources, and contingencies.
The Navajo County Continuity of Government Plan consolidates the most critical and essential
components of the individual departmental COOP plans into a single, coordinated framework. Together,
these plans provide a comprehensive approach to ensuring the continued delivery of county services and
the effective functioning of county government during emergencies.

PROMULGATION STATEMENT 
 
Transmitted herewith is the Continuity of Operations / Continuity of Government (COOP/COG) 
Plan for Navajo County, Arizona. It provides a framework in which Navajo County, Arizona, 
along with its officials, departments, agencies, and other entities, can plan and perform their 
respective essential functions during a disruption, disaster or national emergency. 
 
This Continuity of Operations/Continuity of Government Plan was prepared in accordance with 
direction from Presidential Decision Directive 67, Federal Continuity Directive 1, Federal 
Continuity Directive 2, and Continuity Guidance Circular 1. It is in accordance with other existing 
Federal, State, and local statutes and understanding of the various departments involved. This 
Plan supersedes any previous COOP/COG Plans and has been concurred by the Chairperson 
of Navajo County, Arizona. It will be reviewed annually and re-certified biennial. Recipients are 
requested to advise the Navajo County, Arizona Executive Team of any changes which might 
result in its improvement or increase in its usefulness. 
 
 
 
 
APPROVED: ____________________________              DATE: __________________

<!-- page 80 -->
4  
EXECUTIVE SUMMARY 
 
Navajo County, Arizona recognizes that there are natural, man-made and terrorist threats that 
can impact the ability to perform essential functions that serve government organizations, 
citizens and private business. While the majority of these incidents cannot be prevented, many 
can be mitigated to reduce the impact through preventive measures to protect government 
assets or to rapidly recover from incidents in an organized and coordinated manner. 
 
The key purpose of Continuity of Operations/Continuity of Government (COOP/COG) planning 
is to reduce the consequences of a disaster to acceptable levels and to ensure that Navajo 
County, Arizona has sufficient resources and planning alternatives to continue its essential 
operations. Although when and how a disaster will occur is not known, the fact that future 
disasters will happen is certain. How well (or poorly) the COOP/COG plan is designed and 
implemented will determine the response, recovery, resumption, and restoration capabilities of 
Navajo County, Arizona. 
 
The Navajo County, Arizona Continuity of Government plan, also referred to as "COG" is a 
strategic planning effort that helps ensure that Navajo County, Arizona has sufficient resources 
and planning alternatives to continue its essential operations should facilities and personnel be 
affected by any adverse event such as fire, severe storm, power disturbance/interruption or an 
emergency or disaster due to terrorism, natural or technological hazard. 
 
The Continuity of Government plan serves as the coordination point for the recovery of essential 
functions for Navajo County, Arizona. While each individual organization within Navajo County, 
Arizona develops an individual Continuity of Operations Plan (COOP) to address the functions 
at the organizational level, many resources required by these organizations will be organized, 
prioritized and coordinated by the Executive Team level of Navajo County, Arizona. This plan 
serves to coordinate the decision making process and those key resources for Navajo County, 
Arizona. 
 
Note: The generic term "organization" is used to refer to all entities of County and City 
government. When a specific department, organization, office, board, or commission is 
tasked within the Continuity of Government plan, its official title will be used. 
  
  
COOP vs. COG 
Continuity of Operations Planning (COOP) 
 
Continuity of Operations planning is a planning strategy created within individual organizations 
to ensure their ability to continue the performance of their essential functions during a wide 
range of potential disruptions. Essentially, it is the capability of maintaining the core operations 
and essential functions of their organization under all eventualities. This is accomplished 
through the development of plans, procedures, and provisions for leadership succession, 
essential functions, alternative facilities, personnel, resources, interoperable communications, 
and essential records/databases. Within Navajo County, Arizona, there are 24 distinct 
Continuity of Operations plans that have been developed as an overall framework for the 
establishment of Continuity of Government. Each of these 24 plans is unique in nature specific 
to the organizations structure and operations, and has been tailored to address the following 
key elements of their continuity planning requirements: 
• Essential Functions (Ranked by Priority)

<!-- page 81 -->
5  
• Essential Records / Vital Resources 
• Orders of Succession 
• Delegations of Authority 
• Alternate Facilities 
• COOP Teams and Responsibilities 
• Communications 
• Alert Notification 
• Testing, Training, and Exercises 
Continuity of Government Planning (COG) 
 
This Continuity of Government Plan for Navajo County, Arizona is the summation of the most 
critical and major elements of each of the 24 Continuity of Operations Plans highlighted above. 
As such, this Continuity of Government plan supports a higher level of planning which serves as 
the framework for the preservation, maintenance, or reconstitution of the institution of the overall 
Navajo County, Arizona government. Through the coordination of these 24 individual continuity 
planning strategies and elements within Navajo County, Arizona, the Executive Team has better 
visibility to develop a unified and cohesive Continuity of Government Plan that results in the 
ability to carry out essential functions and operational responsibilities of Navajo County, Arizona.

<!-- page 82 -->
6

PLANNING ASSUMPTIONS 
 
The Continuity of Government plan assumes that all Navajo County, Arizona organizations have 
Continuity plans in place for their organizations and locations necessary to maintain or recover 
essential functions. Organizations are expected to understand their space allocation needs and 
communicate that to the proper continuity team when they don't have the ability to organize their 
own alternate site plan. 
 
This plan assumes that Navajo County, Arizona in coordination with the Navajo County Board of 
Supervisors will form specific Continuity Teams designed to address the situation and meet 
the needs and requirements of Navajo County, Arizona during continuity events.  At a minimum, 
these Continuity Teams will consist of leadership, management, and key decision makers within 
Navajo County, Arizona who are thereby responsible for implementing the Continuity of 
Government plan and its actions as required. 
 
The assumptions listed below serve as a scope of an incident that could occur and what other 
situations may exist that will need to be considered in the recovery of essential functions: 
• An incident or operational disruption has occurred within Navajo County, Arizona which 
impacts the ability to perform or deliver of one or more organization's essential functions. 
• Whatever the incident, the consequences can be summarized to manageable situations 
that Navajo County, Arizona, its organizations, and their private partners can manage. 
• One or more Navajo County, Arizona organizations are becoming overwhelmed in their 
ability to recover from the incident independently. 
• Services provided by private enterprise, local government(s) and/or the federal 
government may be impacted. 
• Power, fuel, water, food, medical, power and telecommunications sources and supply 
chains may be impacted. 
CONTINUITY TEAMS 
 
The activation and implementation of the Continuity of Government plan is performed in 
conjunction with the details of the Navajo County, Arizona Emergency Operations Plan (EOP). 
Policy Support and executive leadership is a vital part of any response and the EOP guidelines 
for Policy Support sets forth the roles and responsibilities as part of the overall Incident 
Command System (ICS). For the Navajo County, Arizona, the Continuity Teams and its 
members act as the primary decision-makers for Policy Support during the activation of 
the COG and for addressing the requirements regarding all COG issues. 
 
In order for Navajo County, Arizona to successfully manage and execute the actions contained 
within this Continuity of Government Plan, it is necessary to develop specific Continuity 
Teams which will have the responsibility in their various areas to oversee the design, strategy, 
and ongoing development and coordination of the Continuity of Government Plan as a whole. In 
addition, Continuity Team members will serve a significant role in the response and decision 
making process of the Continuity of Government plan when disruptions occur. The following are

<!-- page 84 -->
8  
Continuity Teams developed specifically for Navajo County, Arizona: 
 
Executive Team 
The Executive Team consists of the highest ranking officials and key decision makers within an 
organization. This team is designed to create an overarching decision and policy making group 
which plans, assesses, and coordinates the response to events that disrupt continuity of an 
organization's operations. Members selected to serve on the Executive Team should have the 
capacity to represent their respective area of expertise and make sound recommendations 
which serve in the best interest of the organization and its overall operations. At a minimum, the 
Executive Team should be comprised of key representatives from the following types of 
positions and organizations: Executive Management, Safety/Security, Facilities Management, 
Finance, Human Resources, and Information Technology. It is highly recommended that 
Executive Team members review and have a clear understanding of the vital elements 
contained within the various continuity plans for their organization. It is also recommended that 
the Executive Team conduct planning meetings every six months to discuss and update the 
Continuity Plan.

OBJECTIVES 
 
The Navajo County, Arizona COG is designed to address and accomplish the following 
objectives: 
• Ensure uninterrupted command, control, and leadership of Navajo County, Arizona. 
• Protect critical facilities, systems, equipment and records. 
• Become operational within three (3) business days (or sooner) and maintaining 
capability for up to 30 days (or until primary facility is restored to full operation). 
• Resume technology operations and support for time-sensitive business operations in the 
event existing technology processing has been rendered inoperable. 
• Reduce the operational effects of a disaster on time-sensitive business operations 
through a set of pre-defined and flexible procedures to be used in directing recovery 
operations. 
• Resume production processing of the most time-sensitive computer systems, network 
services and applications within three (3) business days (or sooner) following the 
disruptive event. 
• Provide a proper work environment for displaced staff while their facilities and their 
contents are being restored. 
• Resume and maintain adequate service levels to residents and businesses of Navajo 
County, Arizona. 
SCOPE 
 
This plan includes a comprehensive list identifying the time-sensitive and less time-sensitive 
essential functions, automated technology, and support areas for Navajo County, Arizona. This 
plan will be activated in the event any primary facility or a portion of a primary facility is involved

<!-- page 93 -->
17  
in an emergency involving a disruption of operations for three (3) days or more or is declared 
unusable for normal operations. 
 
This plan addresses resumption and recovery in any emergency or disaster situation. It does 
not address building emergency and evacuation procedures or on-site resumption and recovery 
procedures which are addressed in each organizations individual Continuity of Operations plan. 
Actions related to the physical restoration process, in terms of primary site restoration, recovery 
de-activation, migration and reestablishment of normal operations, termination/shutdown of 
recovery operations at alternate sites, integration of supporting activities with other departments 
to ensure essential functions can be performed, and post-recovery operations are also 
addressed in each organization's COOP. 
 
This plan is based on the formal approval of the Supervisor District III of those critical business 
functions and associated support functions identified as time-sensitive. A list of essential 
functions and services provided by each organization of Navajo County, Arizona has been 
arranged in order of priority is documented in their respective COOP's and identifies the 
essential functions operations, essential records and resources, and periods of time for which 
and after which disruptions could result in significant losses to Navajo County, Arizona. 
 
Each summary contained within the Navajo County, Arizona COG shall include: 
• The line of succession for their organization, with a minimum of three alternates. 
• A minimum of two (2) points-of-contact for their organization, including the leadership of 
the organizations and a designated Continuity Coordinator. 
• A list of all essential functions of the organization, arranged in order of priority of those 
critical functions essential to the mission of the organization's operations. 
• A list of Essential Records and Vital resources used by each organization within Navajo 
County, Arizona, including documentation of the protection, duplication and movement of 
these items. 
• A specified Alternate Facility location identified for each Primary Facility where an 
organization operates. 
Additionally, this document serves as a starting point for the recovery of Navajo County, Arizona 
government operations. Included in this document is a list of all participating Navajo County, 
Arizona organizations, Department Heads, Continuity Planning Chiefs and their contact 
information. These people are responsible for developing, maintaining and implementing their 
own organizational level continuity plans with the assistance of the Navajo County Board of 
Supervisors. 
 
While all plans can be overwhelmed by the events presented, this plan attempts to address to 
consequences of an unknown incident by taking into account the needs of the citizens, 
businesses, and Navajo County, Arizona organizations, and how those needs could be met in 
an impacted environment. The goal is to perform as much pre-work in the form of coordination, 
prioritization, alternate work methods, or any other means necessary so that during an incident, 
focus can be on resolving issues instead of making decisions that could have been resolved in 
advance. 
PHASE I: ACTIVATION OF CONTINUITY OF GOVERNMENT PLAN 
 
This plan serves as a coordination document of the resources available to Navajo County,

<!-- page 94 -->
18  
Arizona in a time of disruption or crisis. 
 
Analysis of the situation is important with as many verifiable facts as possible. Status of facilities 
and/or the functions impacted is the outcome of the analysis along with any time frames for 
recovery that the incident will allow. 
 
Once a decision has been made to activate the Navajo County, Arizona Continuity of 
Government plan, the Supervisor District III will execute the plan and coordinate with the 
appropriate Continuity Teams. Each Navajo County, Arizona organization will then be contacted 
to activate their COOP at the direction of the Supervisor District III. 
 
In the event of limited resources, allocation of resources will be made by the Supervisor District 
III or their designee. Each organization in Navajo County, Arizona has designated a specific 
individual to serve as their organization's Continuity Coordinator to communicate directly with 
their internal leadership and provide information and requirements to the Supervisor District III 
on continuity of operations planning. 
 
The support of organizations that perform the most essential functions will be prioritized and 
become the focal point at that time. Relocation of staff, resources and functions are coordination 
activities that will need to be considered as well as the availability of any private sector supplies 
or services such power, water, telecommunications, and fuel. All participating organizations of 
Navajo County, Arizona have identified essential functions as part of their continuity planning 
efforts. With these lists which identify each organization's essential functions, the Navajo 
County, Arizona has the ability to broadly view the overall framework of functions and prioritize 
them based on specific criteria; including life/safety, financial, public perception, and recovery 
time requirements. While this is an objective measure of the priority, subjective decisions can be 
made based on this priority as to a potentially different order of restoration should occur. It is 
also not expected that in any one incident that all functions are impacted to the point of requiring 
restoration. This prioritized list would then be used to identify the functions impacted, what the 
recovery time would be, and what alternative arrangements are going to be put in place so that 
a clear and concise communication can be made to the media and public as to the functions 
impacted. 
PHASE II: ALTERNATE FACILITY AND CONTINUITY OF OPERATIONS 
 
This section speaks to how Navajo County, Arizona will conduct its functions during a Continuity 
Plan activation scenario. 
 
Each Navajo County, Arizona organization shall activate its COOP and understand its place in 
the priority of Navajo County, Arizona functions. 
 
Activation of the plan shall consider life/safety aspects first and that response to the incident 
may take a higher priority than the restoration of services, particularly when organization staff 
members have homes and families impacted by the incident. 
 
Any resource, facility or staff shortages shall be reported to the Supervisor District III or their 
designee. 
PHASE III: RECONSTITUTION / RETURN TO NORMAL OPERATIONS 
 
During Prevention, the primary responsibilities of Navajo County, Arizona organizations include:

<!-- page 95 -->
19  
• Plan to protect employees. 
• Plan for the protection and duplication of Essential Records and Vital Resources. 
• Plan for the efficient resumption of mission essential functions. 
• Plan for and identify potential alternate operating sites. 
• Plan to support and communicate with the Supervisor District III and designated 
Continuity Teams. 
• Plan to streamline the reporting of resumption and recovery progress to the Supervisor 
District III. 
• Provide and maintain a current Continuity of Operations Plan. 
• Review and re-approve Continuity of Operations Plan annually. 
During Response, the primary responsibilities of Navajo County, Arizona organizations include: 
• Establish an immediate and controlled presence for response. 
• Conduct a preliminary assessment of incident impact, known injuries, extent of damage, 
and disruption to the organizations operations and essential functions. 
• Determine if and/or when access to the affected facilities will be allowed. 
• Provide the Supervisor District III with the facts necessary to make informed decisions 
regarding subsequent resumption and recovery activity. 
During Resumption, the primary responsibilities of Navajo County, Arizona organizations 
include: 
• Monitor and report progress of the resumption operations. 
• Notify and appraise the Supervisor District III of the situation. 
• Mobilize and activate the personnel necessary to facilitate the resumption process. 
• Notify employees, vendors and other internal and external individuals and organizations. 
During Recovery, the primary responsibilities of Navajo County, Arizona organizations include: 
• Prepare for and/or implement procedures to facilitate and support the recovery of less 
time sensitive operations. 
• Mobilize additional personnel and support organizations as required. 
• Maintain an information flow regarding the status of recovery operations among 
employees, vendors and other internal and external individuals and organizations. 
During Restoration, the primary responsibilities of Navajo County, Arizona organizations 
include: 
• Manage salvage, repair and/or refurbishment efforts at the affected facility.

<!-- page 96 -->
20  
• Prepare procedures necessary to the relocation or migration of essential functions to the 
new or repaired facility. 
• Implement procedures necessary to mobilize operations, support and technology agency 
relocation. 
• Manage the relocation effort as well as perform employee, vendor, and customer 
notification before, during and after relocation or migration. 
Primary Mission Essential Functions 
Primary Mission Essential Functions for Navajo County Board of Supervisors 
1. Functions to be performed, given a One Day - One Week disruption. (Highest priority to 
lowest): 
• Agendas - Notify Citizens of Meetings 
• Maintain all records 
• Board Meetings to approve documents impacting County business; i.e., 
agreements, appointments, budgets, etc.; and discuss current issues 
• Collect, process and distribute mail to County Departments and process outgoing 
mail from County Departments 
• Approve time sheets 
2. Functions to be performed, given a One Week - One Month disruption. (Highest priority 
to lowest): 
• Continuation of functions listed under previous Tier(s) identified above 
• Minutes - Memorialize meeting proceedings for permanent record for Board of

KEY PERSONNEL 
 
Key personnel are those required to implement the Continuity Plan. These involve the 
leadership and management personnel of the organization and any other personnel as identified 
in the organizations plan. There are logistical staff that assist in setting up and supporting the 
operational staff and functions that the organization performs. There are operations personnel 
who perform the Mission Essential Functions of the organization. There are reconstitution 
personnel that are preparing the impacted site or a whole new site if the damage is severe, for 
operations again. Note that personnel should NOT be assigned double duty on multiple teams 
during a Continuity Plan implementation. Stress levels will be high, burnout will be an issue to 
be dealt with and availability of staff will be impacted post incident. 
ESSENTIAL RECORDS AND RESOURCES 
 
Essential Records, Vital Resources, databases, systems and other elements critical to 
operations are the responsibility of each individual organization to manage, mitigate and 
proactively protect from potential incidents. Mitigation efforts include converting paper records to 
electronic forms, ensuring storage areas are not susceptible to water damage, and ensuring that 
a records retention policy is in place to avoid storing large amounts of records that are outdated 
and beyond their useful life. 
 
Organizations should recognize in their assessment of what records and resources are truly 
vital to their operations. Given the considerable expense in recovering damaged records, 
organizations need to properly assess what is truly vital. Efforts to mitigate destructive effects on 
records will be repaid many times over if an incident occurs. 
 
If there is an incident that damages hardcopy records, the Navajo County IT Department will 
need to assist organizations with document or artifact restoration services.

TEST, TRAINING, AND EXERCISING / PLAN MAINTENANCE 
 
It is necessary for all levels of personnel, including those appointed or elected, to maintain their 
understanding of the goals and objectives of continuity planning; including how the plan affects 
their area, its overall design, and the strategy it employs. Awareness of Continuity Planning best 
practices and the basic discussion areas it addresses is crucial and how it differs from

<!-- page 118 -->
42  
emergency response type plans. 
 
All personnel within Navajo County, Arizona should be tested and trained on their organizations 
plans so they are aware of their organizations COOP and its contents. The process of testing, 
training, and exercising the plans should include, but not limited to the following areas: what are 
the mission essential functions of the organization, what essential records and resources are 
critical for the organization to continue its functions, who are the key leadership personnel within 
the organization and who are their designated alternates, what alternate facilities have been 
identified as potential sites for relocation, and that each employee should have a plan for their 
family in case of emergency. 
 
Tests and exercises can take on a number of forms. The most basic is an orientation that 
resembles a meeting where aspects of the plan are discussed with employees. A test may be of 
a new piece of equipment or procedure. A tabletop exercise is a realistic scenario posed in a 
conference room environment to key people in the organization who are asked to use the plan 
and their own knowledge to respond and recover from the scenario proposed. A functional 
exercise involves the actual use of equipment, moving of people, etc, from one organization, 
facility or division. A full scale exercise is a larger scale event than the functional exercise 
involving a large number of organizations, private sector, local government and/or federal 
government. 
 
Maintenance/Review of the plan shall occur on a quarterly basis. This can occur during a staff 
meeting where staff identifies changes in contact information and function.

Board of Supervisors Regular 3. a. 3.        
Meeting Date: 01/27/2026  
Title: Navajo County Emergency Operations plan 2026-28
Submitted For: Catrina Jenkins, EMP Director 
Submitted By: Catrina Jenkins, EMP Director
Department: NC Public Health Services District Division: Emergency Management
Motion before the Board:
Navajo County Emergency Operations Plan for 2026-2028
Background:
Navajo County Emergency Management works with local, state, Federal, Tribal, private and
non-governmental agencies to develop and update the Navajo County Emergency Operations
Plan (EOP). An Emergency Operations Plan outlines how people and property will be protected
in emergencies and disasters. Key elements of the EOP include Mitigation, Preparedness, Response, and Recovery strategies. The plan is executed
when a declaration has been made by the Board of Supervisors or if it was placed into effect by
the County Manager or other delegated authority. The annual review and approval of this plan is necessary to meet the objectives
of our Emergency Management Program Grant. Key components of the plan were reviewed and updated this year based off of information
obtained through real world incidents and training exercises. Information such as contacts,
response capabilities and more were reviewed for relevance and accuracy. In addition, several
annexes were reviewed and updated, such as the Logistics Management and Resource Support, Mass Care, and Civil Disturbances.

Promulgation Statement 
  
Navajo County, Arizona 
 
In the event of natural, technological or national security disaster affecting the unincorporated 
portions of Navajo County government must be prepared to implement plans and procedures to 
protect lives and property.  In addition, county government must be prepared to provide support 
to municipal governments affected by disaster conditions. 
This plan is published in support of the State of Arizona Emergency Response and Recovery 
Plan.  It supersedes any and all of the Navajo County Emergency Operations Plan's prior.  It is 
in accordance with Arizona Revised Statutes, Title 26, Chapter 2 and the Navajo County 
Emergency Resolution of 2011. 
The purpose of this plan is to provide direction and guidance to Navajo County governmental 
departments and supporting agencies.  It provides guidance to assist county departments in 
preparing for and executing assigned emergency tasks to ensure maximum survival of 
the population and property in the event of a natural or man-made disaster. 
This plan is effective for planning purposes and preparations on receipt.  It will be executed 
when an emergency declaration is made by the Board of Supervisors or when it is placed into 
effect by the County Manager or other delegated authority.

Chairmen of Board of Supervisors

emergency responders, Navajo County governmental departments and supporting agencies to 
effectively coordinate and collaborate, before, during, and after a disaster, in order to provide a 
comprehensive response to all emergencies.

materially affect the overall planning approach and do not radically change responsibilities of 
senior county officials or county departments.  Changes will be recorded in the record of

I. Purpose, Scope, Overview, and Assumptions 
  
A. General 
 
Presidential Homeland Security Directives 5 and 8, enacted in 2004, require the State and Local 
governments to adopt the fundamental principles, language and operational concepts 
embedded in the National Incident Management System (NIMS) and the National Response 
Plan (NRP) as a condition for receiving certain categories of federal support for Emergency 
Management. To meet these requirements, Navajo County created this Emergency Operations 
Plan (EOP) and the Navajo County Board of Supervisors officially adopted it on . 
 
The revised Navajo County EOP is the product of a detailed and focused planning process that 
1) fully incorporates the NIMS concepts, principles, practice and language 2) capitalizes on the 
lessons learned from recent disasters, 3) incorporates plans, programs and policies that have 
emerged since the last revision of the EOP. The EOP establishes a framework through which 
the County may prepare for; respond to; recover from; and mitigate to prevent the impacts of a 
wide variety of disasters that could adversely affect the health, safety and/or general welfare of 
the residents and emergency workers of Navajo County. The EOP provides guidance to Navajo 
County officials or procedures, organization and responsibilities, which will prevent, minimize 
and/or relieve personnel hardship and property damage associated with disasters or the 
imminent threat thereof. This plan also provides for an integrated and coordinated county, 
municipal, state and federal response. This plan is a living document, fully integrated with a 
database and dynamic fields system built and maintained by BOLDplanning. It complies with the 
most current guidance from DHS and FEMA regarding the ability to keep data and personal 
information secure, current, and up to date. 
 
The EOP is operations oriented, and addresses communication and warning systems; rapid 
deployment and pre-deployment resources; evacuation and shelter operations; post disaster 
response and recovery activities. It’s imperative is to clearly define the responsibilities of county, 
municipal, volunteer and other organizations through an Base Plan/Incident Command 
System/Response Annex approach to planning and operations. 
 
The EOP describes the basic strategies, assumptions and mechanics through which the County 
will mobilize resources and conduct activities to guide and support County Emergency 
Management efforts through prevention, preparedness, response, recovery and mitigation. To 
facilitate inter-government operations, the EOP adopts a functional approach that groups the 
type of assistance to be provided under each Annex. Each Annex is headed by a primary 
agency, which has been selected based on its authorities, resources and capabilities in the 
functional area. In addition, other agencies with similar capabilities have been given support 
assignments to appropriate Annex. The Annex serve as the primary operational mechanism 
through which County assistance is managed. Command staff and other General staff have 
been assigned to support the Annex. County assistance will be provided to impacted 
communities within the County under the overall authority of the Navajo County Emergency 
Management, on behalf of the Navajo County Board of Supervisors. 
 
In an effort to ensure that the revised EOP was strictly aligned with the State and National 
preparedness guidance, the Arizona Department of Emergency and Military Affairs and National

<!-- page 168 -->
18  
Department of Homeland Security publications listed below were consulted and closely 
followed: 
• Comprehensive Preparedness Guide (CPG) 101, November 2010 
• Public Assistance Program guidelines (FP-104-009-2, January 2016) 
• Threat and Hazard Identification Guide (THIRA) 201, Second Edition, August 2013 
• National Response Framework (September, 2014) 
• FEMA NIMCAST User's Guide 
• National Planning Scenarios (15) 
• Core Capabilities (February 2015) 
 
  
B. Purpose 
 
The purpose of the Navajo County Emergency Operations Plan is to establish a framework for 
government, non-profit organizations, the private sector, and residents to address prevention, 
protection, preparation, response, recovery and mitigation of the effects of emergencies and 
disasters while providing clear guidance to activate the Navajo County Emergency Operations 
Center (EOC). The ideal life-cycle is shown below: 
  
 
  
C. Scope 
 
This plan identifies when and under what conditions the application, activation or revision of this 
plan is necessary.

<!-- page 169 -->
19  
The plan establishes fundamental policies, strategies and assumptions for a County-
wide program that is guided by the principles of the National Incident Management System. 
This EOP provides the following benefits to Navajo County: 
• Creating a plan which addresses all hazards, all phases of emergency management, all 
impacts, and extends an opportunity to partner with all stakeholders.   
• The EOP establishes a Concept of Operations spanning the direction and control of an 
emergency from initial monitoring through post disaster response, recovery and 
mitigation.   
• The EOP defines inter-agency and inter-government coordination mechanisms to 
facilitate delivery of immediate response and recovery assistance.   
• The EOP assigns specific functions to appropriate County and municipal agencies and 
organizations as well as outlines methods to coordinate with the private sector, volunteer 
organizations, citizens and state and federal counterparts.   
• The EOP identifies actions that County response and recovery organizations will take in 
coordination with municipal, state and federal counterparts as appropriate, regardless of 
the magnitude of the disaster.

Each agency was consulted with to determine their particular emergency roles and 
responsibilities. Each agency has agreed with the responsibilities assigned to them in the 
Navajo County EOP. Agency concurrence signatures are maintained with the Navajo County 
Emergency Management. The EOP's concepts were developed by the Navajo County 
Emergency Management, in coordination with the agencies and organizations involved in 
emergency management activities. Each agency and organization involved is expected to have 
its own procedures to implement the concept of operations. 
 
Each of the above listed agencies will receive "Viewer Access" to the Navajo County EOP via 
the BOLDplanning System, ReadyNavajoCounty.com. 
 
In addition: 
• The Navajo County  EOP is adopted by governing bodies and by resolution, which 
serves as the promulgation letter for the EOP. A copy of the signed promulgation is 
found in Section I: E Acceptance, Signatures and Proof of Maintenance. 
• A Record of Changes Log is used to record all published changes as those holding 
copies of the EOP receive them. The holder of the copy is responsible for making the 
appropriate changes and updating the Log.  
• A master copy of the EOP, with a master Record of Changes Log, is maintained in the 
Navajo County Emergency Management. 
1. Planning Process 
 
The process used by Navajo County has been designed to ensure that all stakeholders have an 
opportunity to participate in the development of the EOP and the EOP is based on the best 
information available. To this end, the planning process is based on the following planning 
principles: 
• Planning should be community-based, representing the whole community and their 
needs

<!-- page 174 -->
24  
• Planning should include participation from all stakeholders in the community 
• Planning uses a logical and analytical problem-solving process to help address the 
complexity and uncertainty inherent in potential hazards 
• Planning considers all hazards and threats 
• Planning should be flexible enough to address both traditional and catastrophic incidents 
• Time, uncertainty, risk and experience influence planning 
• Effective plans tell those with operational responsibilities what to do and why to do it 
• Planning is fundamentally a process to manage risk 
• Planning is one of the key components of the preparedness cycle of planning, 
organizing, training, equipping, exercising, evaluating, and taking corrective actions 
2. Implementation of NIMS 
 
The Navajo County EOP implements the Incident Command System (ICS) and the National 
Incident Management System (NIMS) as mandated by Homeland Security Presidential Directive 
5 (HSPD-5) and Presidential Policy Directive 8 (PPD-8) by: 
• Using ICS and the multi-agency coordination system to manage and support all 
incidents 
• Integrating all response agencies and entities into a single, seamless system 
• Establishing a public information plan in the Annex dealing with dissemination of 
information. 
• Identifying and characterizing resources according to established standards and types 
• Requiring all personnel to be trained properly for the job they perform 
• Ensuring interoperability, accessibility and redundancy of communications

<!-- page 175 -->
25  
 II. Situation 
 
This section of the plan summarizes the hazards that could potentially affect Navajo County. 
The hazards and risk analysis addresses the major hazards to which the County is vulnerable; 
provides a summary of the County's population with access and functional needs (AFN); 
outlines the assumptions that were considered in the planning process; and defines disaster 
magnitude classifications that will trigger County response under the NIMS. 
 
A comprehensive hazard and risk assessment is contained in the Navajo County mitigation 
plan. The plan is kept under separate cover and can be accessed by contacting Navajo County 
Emergency Management. 
  
A. Hazard Analysis 
 
Hazard and Vulnerability Assessment Summary 
 
Navajo County is vulnerable to a wide range of hazards that threaten its communities, 
businesses and environment. To determine the hazards that pose the greatest threat, Navajo 
County has prepared a Threat Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment. The major findings 
are summarized below. The assessment was developed from historical data of events that have 
occurred, and specifically examines:  
1. Probability (frequency) of event 
2. Magnitude of event 
3. Expected warning time before event 
4. Expected duration of event 
For emergency management planning purposes, the critical analysis that must be undertaken is 
an assessment of the consequences of each hazard, including potential area of impact, 
population exposed and impacted, duration of the hazard, and potential economic 
consequences. These rankings utilize the criteria laid out in the Threat and Hazard Identification 
and Risk Assessment (THIRA) to weight them proportionally through historic data as well as 
future projections based on economic, demographic, the critical infrastructure information. 
 
Three levels of risk have been identified: High, Moderate and Low. 
 
High - High probability of occurrence; at least 50 percent or more of population at risk from 
hazard; significant to catastrophic physical impacts to buildings and infrastructure; major loss or 
potential loss of functionality to all essential facilities (hospital, police, fire, EOC and shelters). 
 
Moderate - Less than 50 percent of population at risk from hazard; moderate physical impacts 
to buildings and infrastructure; moderate potential for loss of functionality to essential facilities. 
 
Low - Low probability of occurrence or low threat to population; minor physical impacts.

2. Disaster Magnitude Class 
 
This is an all-hazards EOP and addresses minor, major and catastrophic disasters. These 
levels of disaster are defined as: 
 
Catastrophic Disaster: A disaster that will require massive State and Federal assistance, 
including immediate military involvement. Federal assistance will involve response as well as 
recovery assets. 
 
Major Disaster: A disaster that will likely exceed local capability and require a broad range of 
State and Federal assistance. The Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) will be 
notified and potential Federal assistance will be predominantly recovery oriented. 
 
Minor Disaster: A disaster that will likely be within the response capability of local government 
and will result in only a minimal need for State or Federal assistance. 
  
B. Capability Assessment 
 
Currently capability assessments are performed by local preparedness teams in Arizona. The 
capability assessment is performed in coordination with Department of Homeland Security & 
Emergency Management with wide input accepted from key stakeholders. The results of the 
capability assessment guide future investments in planning, training, exercising and resources. 
The local capability assessment is available under separate cover and is attached to the file 
archive in the BOLDplanning Super System. 
 
Capability Targets are developed in accordance with THIRA guidelines, resulting in 
comprehensive Capability Estimation rankings.
